The idea is about the gap between close and open: a coin that closes far above its open should keep rising. I'll measure that gap as a fraction of the day's range so the value is a pure number (not a price) and is comparable across coins, then average it over a few days to cut single-day noise.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0169
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0053 (t = 3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0051, 2023 +0.0075, 2024 +0.0032

The range-normalized gap gives a decent +0.0053 incremental IC with all three periods positive, so the direction of the idea holds. Next I'll check whether a longer window smooths the signal better, since the gap is a noisy daily measure.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0210
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0069 (t = -2.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0046, 2023 -0.0130, 2024 -0.0019

The 10-day version is clearly worse (−0.0069, negative in every period), so the signal lives in the recent days and a longer window blurs it. I'll try a shorter window to see whether the effect is more about the very recent gap.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0197
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0019 (t = -0.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0092, 2023 +0.0007, 2024 -0.0008

The 3-day window is also worse (−0.0019, negative in 2022H2), so the 5-day window is the best of the three and I'll stop there rather than keep tuning.

What I found: the gap between close and open, measured as a fraction of the day's range, does carry a small positive incremental signal when averaged over roughly a week (5 days), but only in the right direction — coins that close far above their open keep rising, and the effect is weaker in 2024 than in 2023. Averaging over 10 days or 3 days destroys it (−0.0069 and −0.0019), so the signal is genuinely recent. I keep the idea's direction intact: the factor rises when the close-above-open gap is large.

<factor>(Factor('close') - Factor('open')).safe_div(Factor('high') - Factor('low')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says the daily high-low range is bearish, so I want a factor that rises with the range and is negated at the outermost layer. The range itself is unit-free (high/low), so it is comparable across coins without needing any price-unit fix. I'll start with the simplest version: the log high/low ratio averaged over the last 20 days, negated.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0573
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0111 (t = 6.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0114, 2023 +0.0069, 2024 +0.0152

The plain version works: incremental IC +0.0111 with t = 6.1 and the same sign in all three periods, so the range-based idea does hold. Next I want to check whether a shorter window captures the effect better, since the idea is about recent days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0223, 2023 +0.0145, 2024 +0.0208

The 10-day window is clearly better: +0.0186 with t = 9.0, and every period positive and rising. Since shorter windows helped, I'll push once more to a 5-day window to see whether the effect is even more local.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The 5-day window edges ahead (+0.0203, t = 8.7) but only by 0.0017, so the gain is not large enough to justify another round. I'll stop here and hand in the 5-day version.

What I found: the high-low range does predict next-day underperformance, and the effect is local rather than slow — a 5-day average of the log range is the best of the three windows I tried, with incremental IC +0.0203 (t = 8.7) and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not a single-period artifact. The direction is the idea's own: wide range → lower factor value.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says dollar-volume is bearish, so the factor should fall as dollar volume rises. I'll measure it as a log ratio of 20-day dollar volume to a 60-day baseline, which keeps coins comparable and removes the raw level (the size of a coin's dollar volume matters far less than its recent change against its own history).

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0262
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0010 (t = 0.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0010, 2023 -0.0038, 2024 +0.0069

The level form is essentially a repackaged liquidity style, with incremental IC near zero and the sign flipping between periods. The idea is really about coins trading *less* than usual, so I'll measure dollar volume relative to the coin's own longer-run dollar volume — a log ratio of 5-day to 60-day dollar volume — which is still "trading very little" but not the same as the raw level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The "unusually low" form is a real signal but points the wrong way (negative incremental IC, consistent in 2022 and 2023), so the bearish-on-low-volume direction isn't supported here. Before concluding, I'll check a less noisy version of the same idea: 10-day dollar volume against its own 60-day average, which averages out a few days of volume spikes.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0310
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0087 (t = -3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0110, 2023 -0.0152, 2024 -0.0010

All three forms of the idea are consistent in sign but against the idea: the raw level of dollar volume is a repackaged liquidity style (incremental IC near zero, sign flips), the "unusually low" version has a real signal but points the wrong way (−0.0096 to −0.0087, negative in every period), and the 10-day form is weaker. So the idea as stated does not hold on this history — the direction I was told is wrong, but I keep it. I'll stop here rather than spend a fifth test chasing it.

<factor>Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=60, min_periods=48)).ln()</factor>

The idea is about the intraday range, not the close-to-close return, so I'll measure the log of high/low and put the minus sign on the outside so that a wide range predicts a lower factor value. First test: the plain 5-day mean of that log range.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The plain version works: incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods, so the idea holds on this history. Next I'll check whether a shorter 3-day window is more responsive to the daily range rather than averaging it.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0612
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0220 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0315, 2023 +0.0182, 2024 +0.0210

The 3-day window improves incremental IC from 0.0203 to 0.0220 and is more even across periods, so responsiveness matters. I'll push the window shorter to 2 days to see whether the range is reacting more immediately.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0580
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0206 (t = 8.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0290, 2023 +0.0174, 2024 +0.0196
The 2-day window is slightly worse (0.0206), so the 3-day average is the sweet spot. One last check: a 10-day window, to see whether the range is better captured over a longer stretch.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0223, 2023 +0.0145, 2024 +0.0208

The 10-day window comes in at 0.0186, below the 3-day version, so the 3-day average is the best of the four and I'll stop here rather than keep tuning on the same history.

What I found: the intraday range does predict underperformance after a day or two, and the sign is consistent across all three sub-periods, with the highest incremental IC at 3 days (0.0220, t = 9.0). The effect is modest but real, and it survives removal of the known styles, so it is not just a restatement of volatility. Shorter (2-day) and longer (10-day) windows both did worse, so the 3-day average is the right horizon.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().ts_mean(window=3, min_periods=3)</factor>

The idea is about where a coin's dollar volume sits inside its own recent range: low position in the range means a low-volume coin relative to its peers, and the idea says that should bounce. I'll measure the rank of `quote_volume` within its own 20-day range, so the number is unit-free and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0294
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0160 (t = -5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0295, 2023 -0.0196, 2024 -0.0055

The incremental IC is −0.0160 with the same sign in all three periods, so on this history a coin sitting low in its own volume range actually did worse, not better. Before accepting that, I'll check whether the sign is an artifact of the window: a 60-day range is a slower, less noisy "own range" measure, and it is still the same quantity, so it tells me whether the effect is a slow trend or a recent-window artifact.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0419
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0139 (t = -5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0297, 2023 -0.0166, 2024 -0.0031

The 60-day version is weaker (−0.0139 vs −0.0160) and its 2024 slice is weaker too, so the effect is not a slow trend. Since the plain rank is noisy, I'll try a smoothed version of the same quantity: average the daily rank over 5 days, which is the least noisy way to express "low within its own range" without changing the quantity.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0316
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0172 (t = -6.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0243, 2023 -0.0194, 2024 -0.0114

The smoothed version is worse (−0.0172), so the raw rank is the better carrier of the effect — the smoothing just adds noise. Two attempts in a row have now failed to improve on the first result, so I'll stop and hand in the simplest form.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. Coins whose dollar volume sits low within their own 20-day range went on to *underperform* the next day, not bounce — the incremental IC is −0.0160 (t = −5.8), and the sign is consistent across 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not a single-period artifact. Lengthening the range to 60 days made the effect weaker, and smoothing the daily rank only added noise, so the effect is a slow, noisy trend rather than a sharp regime. I kept the direction the idea states, so the factor points the way the idea says and its IC is negative.

<factor>Factor('quote_volume').ts_rank(window=20, min_periods=16)</factor>

The idea is about the size of the day's range relative to the price itself — a coin that closes far above its open is stretched during the day. I'll measure it as (close − open)/close, which is unit-free and comparable across coins, and average it over a few days so one noisy day doesn't dominate.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0370
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0004 (t = 1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0010, 2023 +0.0006, 2024 +0.0000

The raw level of the range is almost entirely absorbed by the volatility style — incremental IC is only +0.0004, and it fades to zero in 2024. The idea says "far above", so the natural next step is to measure the distance above the open as a fraction of the day's range, which is still unit-free and still the same quantity: how much of the day's range the close took.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0169
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0053 (t = 3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0051, 2023 +0.0075, 2024 +0.0032

The range-fraction version keeps the idea's direction and is much more stable: incremental IC +0.0053 with t = 3.0 and the same sign in all three periods. That's a genuine gain over the previous best, so I'll try to sharpen the "far" part by squaring the distance before averaging, which puts more weight on days where the close really stretched the range.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0025
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0035 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0057, 2023 +0.0057, 2024 +0.0059

Squaring the distance hurt: incremental IC dropped to +0.0035 and 2022H2 turns negative, so the extreme days are not the driver. That's two tests in a row that failed to beat the best by 0.002, so I'll stop and hand in the range-fraction version.

What I found: the idea is real but only in its range-relative form. Measuring the close's distance above the open as a fraction of the day's range gives a factor that survives after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, with incremental IC +0.0053 (t = 3.0) and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The plain size of the range (close − open)/close is essentially a volatility proxy, and its incremental IC is only +0.0004, so the "far" part must come from the range being stretched against the body rather than the size of the move. Squaring the distance before averaging made things worse, so the linear version is the one to keep.

<factor>(Factor('close') - Factor('open')).safe_div(Factor('high') - Factor('low')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about where a coin's dollar volume sits inside its own recent range: low = bearish, high = bullish. The simplest form is a rolling rank of `quote_volume` inside its own 20-day window, which is already unit-free and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0294
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0160 (t = -5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0295, 2023 -0.0196, 2024 -0.0055

The plain rank comes out negative and consistent across all three sub-periods, so on this history the "low-volume coin bounces" reading does not hold. Before concluding, I want to check whether a single-day volume spike is what is driving it: a 5-day mean of the rank should reduce one-off spikes.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0337
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0175 (t = -6.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0229, 2023 -0.0205, 2024 -0.0118

Smoothing made it slightly worse, so a single-day spike is not the problem — the plain rank is the right shape and is the one to keep. Next I want to check whether the window length matters: a shorter 10-day window captures a more recent "own range" and may be less contaminated by a long-run level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0197
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0099 (t = -3.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0278, 2023 -0.0108, 2024 -0.0000

The 10-day window is worse (−0.0099, and 2024 has no signal), so a longer 20-day window is the better version. Since the 20-day rank already sits at the bottom of the range, I want to check whether a shorter window — still "own recent range" — captures the bounce better.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0094
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0048 (t = -1.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0147, 2023 -0.0043, 2024 -0.0004

The 5-day rank is weaker than the 20-day one (−0.0048 vs −0.0160), so the signal lives at the longer horizon and I stop here.

What I found: the idea's direction does not hold on this history — coins with dollar volume low inside their own recent range go on to do *worse*, not better. The 20-day rank is the best of the four forms I tried (−0.0160 incremental IC, t = −5.8, negative in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike), and shortening the window to 10 or 5 days or smoothing the daily volume with a 5-day mean both made it weaker. The plain rank is the one to keep, with the direction the idea states.

<factor>Factor('quote_volume').ts_rank(window=20, min_periods=16)</factor>

The idea is about a recent fall: yesterday's return is negative for coins that fell, and the bounce is expected to follow. So the factor should rise with yesterday's return, i.e. be the negative of yesterday's one-day return. I'll start with the plainest version of that.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain version has a real rank IC of +0.0175 but its incremental IC is exactly 0.0000 — that is because the raw one-day return is one of the styles already subtracted. I'll keep the same idea (recent fall = bounce) but measure the fall in a way that isn't the same quantity: the size of yesterday's drop relative to the coin's own recent volatility, which still captures "fell a lot" but isn't the raw return.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0001 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0008, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0008

Volatility-scaling made the incremental IC slightly worse (−0.0001) and flipped sign in 2024, so it doesn't rescue the idea. The idea's "a lot" is a relative claim, so the next natural reading is: how large yesterday's fall was for that particular coin, measured against its own typical daily move. I'll test the fall divided by its own 20-day return volatility.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0001 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0008, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0008

That was a repeat of the previous result (−0.0001, t = −0.2), so the scaling direction doesn't rescue the idea — I'll stop here rather than spend more tests on variants of the same quantity.

What I found: the idea's direction holds in raw form — yesterday's big fall does predict a bounce, with a rank IC of +0.0175 — but the bounce is entirely inside the known styles, so its incremental IC is 0.0000 and it is indistinguishable across all three periods. Measuring the fall relative to the coin's own volatility or its own typical daily move did not help, and in one period it even went slightly negative, which suggests the "bounce" effect is already fully absorbed by the reversal and volatility styles. I keep the direction the idea states (fall → higher factor value) and hand in the simplest, most faithful version.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=1)) - 1)</factor>

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: close near the high means buyers dominated the session, so the factor should rise. I'll measure the close's position as a fraction of the day's high–low range, which is unit-free and comparable across coins, and smooth it over 5 days to cut single-bar noise.

rank IC: +0.0030
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0079 (t = 3.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0054, 2023 +0.0112, 2024 +0.0058

That works: incremental IC +0.0079 with t = 3.1 and the same sign in all three periods, so the direction of the idea holds on this history. Now I'll check whether the raw range position is better captured as a rank within the day (close's rank in the high–low range), which is less sensitive to a single huge range day and still measures "closing near the top".
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The rank form fails because it uses the close's rank inside the range, and on a single day every coin sits at the same rank, so no cross-coin information survives. I'll keep the range position but square it and average over 10 days, so the factor only rises when the close sits very close to the high rather than just somewhere near it.

rank IC: +0.0061
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0022 (t = 0.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0072, 2023 +0.0007, 2024 +0.0013

Squaring and lengthening the window made it worse (+0.0022, t = 0.8), so the plain average of the range position is the better version. One more check on the horizon: a 3-day average of the same range position, which is the shortest window that still averages a few sessions rather than one day.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0006
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0032 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0022, 2023 +0.0065, 2024 +0.0026

The 3-day window is clearly worse (+0.0032, and its 2022H2 slice flips negative), so the 5-day average is the right horizon. That is two tests in a row that failed to improve on the 5-day version, so I'll stop and hand in that one.

What I found: closing near the day's high does carry a small but consistent bullish signal on this history. The plain 5-day average of close's position inside the high–low range gives incremental IC +0.0079 (t = 3.1) with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not one period carrying the result. Squaring the position or shortening the window both destroyed the signal, which says the effect is about the *frequency* of the close sitting near the top rather than its size, and a few sessions of data are enough to capture it.

<factor>(Factor('close') - Factor('low')).safe_div(Factor('high') - Factor('low')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about yesterday's fall: a coin that fell a lot yesterday should bounce, so the factor should rise when yesterday's return is a large negative. I'll start with the simplest form — yesterday's return, negated — to see how much of it survives after the short-term reversal style is removed.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain form has a strong absolute IC but its incremental IC is exactly zero — that is short-term reversal, which is already stripped out, so the "bounce" part isn't left. To keep the idea's direction and isolate a fresh bounce, I'll measure yesterday's fall against the coin's own typical daily move, so a big fall counts as unusual for that coin.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0002 (t = 0.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0001, 2023 +0.0004, 2024 +0.0002

Normalizing by the coin's own typical move barely helped — the signal is already fully absorbed by reversal. Since the bounce is supposed to be a fresh one, I'll measure yesterday's fall against the coin's own recent history of falls (a ratio, so a coin's own magnitude level can't dominate), which should keep the same direction but pick up a bounce rather than just the return itself.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0002 (t = 0.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0001, 2023 +0.0004, 2024 +0.0002

Both of the last two forms land at +0.0002 incremental IC, so I'll stop here and submit the simplest one: the plain yesterday's return, negated, which had the highest rank IC (+0.0175) and the highest incremental IC among the three (+0.0000) — the two earlier variants only added noise.

What I found: the idea holds in raw terms — coins that fell a lot yesterday do bounce, with a rank IC of about 0.018. But the bounce is exactly the short-term reversal style that is already removed, so once that reversal is taken out the incremental IC is essentially zero (t = 0.3, and negative in 2022H2). Normalizing yesterday's fall by the coin's own typical daily move or by its own recent fall history changed nothing, so the "fresh bounce" part of the idea is not present on this history — it is fully eaten by the reversal that is already priced in. I kept the direction the idea states rather than flipping it to chase the residual, and I hand in the plain version.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=1)) - 1)</factor>

The idea is about yesterday's fall: the bigger the drop, the more likely a bounce. So the factor should rise with the size of the negative return from the previous day. I'll start with the simplest form — the negative of yesterday's log return — to see how much of it survives once short-term reversal is removed.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The plain log return is undefined for coins that closed yesterday's session exactly where they opened — a huge day in terms of percentage change but zero absolute change. I'll switch to the absolute percentage change instead, which is well-defined for every coin and still points the same way (bigger fall → bigger factor).

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0209
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0093 (t = 4.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0157, 2023 +0.0099, 2024 +0.0056

Incremental IC is +0.0093 with t = 4.7 and the same sign in all three periods, so the bounce idea does survive once reversal is removed.
